paras: The attempted lynching of Major Hicks took place on the night of December 17, 1880, when an armed crowd from Ludlow, Kentucky, besieged the jail at Covington to seize Hicks, a Black youth held on suspicion of murdering a white railway worker. The city marshal's guard refused to give him up, a few shots were fired, and the crowd dispersed after midnight. Hicks was later tried, convicted and legally hanged at Covington in February 1882.

On the evening of December 15, 1880, Henry Williams, a young man employed at the Southern Railway shops at Ludlow, was found in a ditch beside the road to the ferry landing with head wounds and his pockets rifled; he died the next day. Police arrested a Black man first named as "Gibson, or Micks" after he paid for boots with a $20 gold piece, and blood and hair were reported on the shoes he left behind.

By the forenoon of December 17 a dispatch described Ludlow as "terribly excited" over evidence that "Major Hicks, a colored boy" was the killer, and predicted that he would be lynched once the town was convinced.

That night, according to the Cincinnati wire report, 150 to 200 men gathered in a barn to plan the lynching of Hicks, who was then in the Covington jail. Marshal Goodsen (spelled Goodson in one version) moved Hicks to the most secure cell, posted his fifteen-man police force armed with revolvers at the jail's only entrance, and organized fifteen armed citizens to patrol outside.

At midnight a force from Ludlow, "armed in all conceivable ways," arrived and demanded Hicks's release, which the marshal refused. No organized attack followed, though a few shots were fired, and by 1:15 a.m. reports said the crowd was dispersing. The Washington Evening Star's short account credited "the sheriff" and a posse, rather than the marshal, with keeping the crowd out.

No arrests of anyone in the crowd appear in the coverage, but Hicks was indicted, and a Cincinnati correspondent wrote in March 1881 that "circumstances favorable to Hicks' innocence" had led a prominent Kentucky lawyer to defend him. The "colored citizens of Cincinnati and vicinity" were asked to attend a benefit concert to pay for the defense, but the event was poorly attended and raised little.

On March 19, 1881, a jury at Covington found Hicks guilty of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to hang. After the Kentucky Court of Appeals refused a new trial, his counsel planned an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court because no Black men had been included in the jury panel. He was resentenced in December 1881, respited by Governor Blackburn because of smallpox, and hanged inside a brick enclosure at Covington on February 24, 1882, before about three hundred admitted spectators. The hanging report noted that there were no living witnesses to the crime and that a priest's statement on the scaffold was his only confession.

Coverage of the jail siege came from a single Cincinnati wire dispatch that ran on December 18 in papers from St. Paul to Wheeling and Washington. Headline writers gave it varied treatment: the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer used "BOUND TO HANG HICKS" and called him "a Murderer," while the St. Paul Daily Globe listed an "Attempt to Lynch a Negro at Covington, Ky." among its "Tales of Horror." The Chicago Tribune's deck spoke of "Covington, Ky., People Thirsty for the Life of a Colored Murderer," and its dispatches called Hicks "the veritable assassin" and "a worthless character" before any trial.

The Evening Star, by contrast, headed its item "LYNCHING PREVENTED" and described Hicks as "accused." The Indianapolis Leader, whose Cincinnati column addressed the city's "colored" community, was the only paper in the coverage to question his guilt, writing that he was "poor, friendless and only eighteen years of age" and might lose his life for a crime he had not committed. When Hicks was convicted, the New-York Tribune called the murder "so cold-blooded" that it explained the "determined but unsuccessful effort" to lynch him.
Most reports credit the Covington marshal and his police with defending the jail, while the Evening Star names the sheriff and a posse.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Major Hicks
bases: An armed crowd from Ludlow went to the Covington jail at night and demanded a Black prisoner accused of murder in order to lynch him, but was refused and dispersed (A7, A11, A12).

A crowd of 150 to 200 men acting without authority sought to lynch Hicks for an alleged murder, but the marshal's guard kept them out and no one was killed (A7, A9, A12); Hicks was later tried and legally hanged in 1882 (A21, A32), so the episode is an attempted lynching.

The Cincinnati wire account (A7, A12) is matched by the Chicago Tribune's separate summary (A11), the Evening Star (A9), the Wilmington Daily Republican (A17), and a Cincinnati correspondent's later reference to 'the attempt to lynch Hicks at the Covington jail' (A18).

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Cincinnati dispatch under headlines such as 'BOUND TO HANG HICKS' and 'Suicide and Mob Law', calling Hicks 'the negro Hicks' and 'a Murderer'.
The Chicago Tribune's deck read 'Covington, Ky., People Thirsty for the Life of a Colored Murderer' and its dispatch called Hicks 'the veritable assassin' before trial.
The Evening Star headed its item 'LYNCHING PREVENTED' and called Hicks 'accused'.
The Indianapolis Leader's Cincinnati column urged support so Hicks could escape a gallows to which he 'may otherwise be unjustly sentenced'.
